doc.title: Ed Polcer interviewed by Monk Rowe, Tarrytown, New York, October 31, 1998

chapter: Swing Street shows and the business
title: The Magic of Swing Street: 52nd Street show and Condon's closing
summary: After touring Condon's show he created Swing Street, about 52nd Street from 1935 to 1955, and brought it to jazz festivals.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Night at Eddie Condon’s.” And we toured for three -- two years with that. And we must have hit maybe 120 different concerts just doing that. And I went to the people at Columbia Artists and said I’d like another go-around and I’ve got a great idea for another show that we could do and they came up with the title, “The Magic of Swing Street.” I said you know we could show going beyond what — “A Night at Eddie Condon’s” described what went on at Eddie Condon’s and it showed the influences of all the influences coming from all over the country to come into that Chicago style playing that we had whether it was Benny Moten. Anyway, it looked at jazz from the influences on the music that was played at Eddie Condon’s. So this other was hey, come and take a walk with us down New York Swing Street. There was only one time in the history of the world where all the forms of classic jazz was played. This is my opening line. And it was New York’s 52nd Street, Swing Street, for 20 years from 1935 to 1955. What was played there? Traditional. Dixieland. Ragtime. New Orleans. Blues. Chicago style. Mainstream. Bebop. Where it was like an artist’s colony for musicians, and it really must have been. I only caught the tail end of it, but I mean to walk down that street there were 40 jazz clubs in two city blocks, and for twenty years music poured forth on this street and musicians could learn from each other. The style of swing reached its maturity there. The traditionalists could hear the swing players, they could hear the bebop players, they could feed off one another. And it was just a wonderful time to be. And when you get into some of the songs that came out of that time, I mean some people in the audience I mean would be in tears. It encompassed World War II for crying out loud, we had some of the prettiest and saddest love songs ever written. And the jazz bands were playing those too. And some of the people, the more elderly ones in the audience, would remember what it was like in the 40s. And whether they’d been to New York or not, I was giving them, we were giving them a trip to New York here in your own armchair in your own, in Cut Bank Shelby, Montana. So that’s in a way it’s a hook and it provided wonderful work for our bands and wonderful chance — Condon’s closed in ‘85, they tore it down to make way for another office building, so that motivated me to, if you can’t come to my club to hear us, I’ll try to bring it to you. And again it goes beyond just a jazz concert. It’s got a little story that goes with it. And people, even the jazz fans, I’ve done this at some of the jazz festivals, and in the face of just pretty what should I say laid-back jazz musicians, I decided I was not going to worry about, I’d have the courage of my convictions and I’d go and say look can I do a set of “The Magic of Swing Street” at one of these jazz festivals. And they said yeah why don’t you. So I do my hour set and people would come up afterwards, even the hard core jazz fans, that was great, I didn’t know that, you said this story here, that was a great story. I didn’t know that about Count Basie and the air conditioner and how he became famous because they decided if they booked the Basie
